summary: SPHEREx SWIPE serves as an open citizen science website that transforms NASA's extensive 102-band near-infrared all-sky observations (0.75–5.00 µm) into a simple, interactive discovery platform. Given that SPHEREx catalogs more than a billion celestial bodies every six months, astronomers encounter significant data overload and high rates of false positives when identifying transient or moving objects. Our platform addresses this challenge by letting users pan and zoom into sky regions with telescope like controls while comparing six-month epochs. Using real astronomical tools such as an automated Blink Comparator, Temporal RGB color-coding, and image differencing (T₁ - T₀) alongside 102-channel spectral data from SPHEREx’s six detectors (revealing molecular signatures like water ice at 3.05 µm, CO₂ at 4.26 µm, and methane), users inspect the field and classify candidates with a single swipe or keystroke (Static Sky, Brightness Change, or Moving Object). SPHEREx SWIPE holds significance because it makes infrared astrophysics accessible to the general public, channeling public enthusiasm into a structured consensus filter that facilitates the identification of asteroids, interstellar comets, nearby brown dwarfs, and variable stars.
details:
SPHEREx SWIPE is an interactive, educational citizen-science web platform inspired by NASA’s SPHEREx space mission. It guides users from mission engineering to active astronomical discovery. First, users complete interactive mission stages where they assemble the space telescope, calibrate its instruments, and execute orbital deployment tasks such as telescope orientation and solar panel extension. Once the mission is unlocked, users access four scientific modules: SPHEREx Map (exploring 36 celestial regions across 102 infrared bands), Compare Years (a multi-epoch blink comparator and time slider to spot moving objects and brightness variations), Star Hunter & Album (identifying and cataloging variable stars), and Case File 09: Planet Nine (an evidence-based investigation into the hypothetical planet beyond Neptune). By clicking any luminous source, users can also extract its 102-band infrared spectrum in real time to identify chemical signatures like water ice, CO₂ and methane.

The platform bridges the gap between complex infrared astrophysics and the general public. Rather than being passive spectators, students, educators, and enthusiasts experience how a real space observatory operates while contributing to a crowd-sourced consensus filter that helps isolate genuine celestial phenomena from false positives. Its intended impact is to spark scientific curiosity, build critical thinking (distinguishing unconfirmed hypotheses like Planet Nine from confirmed data), and democratize access to multi-spectral astronomy.

The application was built as a lightweight, zero-install web platform using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript. We implemented Three.js (r128) with custom shaders to render interactive 3D star fields and the Planet Nine scenario, HTML Canvas for real-time 102-channel spectral curves and minimaps, and localStorage to save user progression, XP, streaks, and collectible discoveries. Official scientific datasets, visual references, and spectral parameters were sourced from NASA Science, JPL-Caltech, and NASA/IPAC IRSA.

Our creativity lies in combining a gamified mission-engineer onboarding with a fast, intuitive "swipe-style" astronomical classifier and interactive spectrometer. During development, our team prioritized genuine hands-on engagement over passive button-clicking, cross-device accessibility (desktop and touchscreen support, three interface view modes, and prefers-reduced-motion compatibility), and strict scientific transparency—clearly distinguishing official NASA imagery from visual recreations and educational simulations.
